articles.description:
Introduction to Golang Profiling with pprof


Profiling Go applications is not just a debugging exercise—it’s a survival skill in modern software development. As Go’s runtime schedules goroutines onto OS threads, the system’s efficiency hinges on how well these threads are utilized. pprof, Go’s built-in profiling tool, acts as a microscope, capturing runtime data via sampling to expose CPU, memory, block, and mutex behaviors. Without it, performance issues like high CPU usage or memory leaks remain invisible, silently degrading application reliability and scalability.
Consider CPU usage: inefficient algorithms or busy-waiting loops force the CPU to execute redundant instructions, consuming cycles that could be allocated to other tasks. pprof’s CPU profiles reveal this by sampling the call …
articles.title: Resolving Go Application Performance Issues: CPU Usage and Memory Leaks with pprof and Flame Graphs

articles.author: Binary Dose
articles.description:
The Producer-Consumer Problem


In concurrent systems, multiple threads produce and consume data through a fixed-size shared buffer.
mutex = 1: Protects critical section.
empty = N: Blocks producer when buffer is full.
full = 0: Blocks consumer when buffer is empty.
Explore the interactive step-by-step buffer visualizer on Binary Dose.
articles.title: The Bounded Buffer Problem: Why Mutex Locks Aren't Enough

articles.author: Dennis Wachira
articles.description:
After receiving my hospital records dataset and understanding its structure, the next step was data cleaning.
Before performing any analysis, it is important to ensure that the data is accurate, consistent and ready to produce reliable insights.
For this phase of the project, I worked on preparing the dataset using Microsoft Excel.
One important practice I learned is to always keep the original dataset untouched.
I created a new worksheet named Cleaned Data by copying the original records. All cleaning activities were performed on this new worksheet while keeping the raw data available for reference.
The following steps were performed:
✅ Checked for duplicate records
Reviewed the dataset for duplicate entries.
No duplicate records were found.
✅ Checked for missing values
Examined all columns for blank cells.
No missing values were identified.
✅ Improved data formatting
Converted the Phone Number column into a numerical format.
Formatted the Bill Amount column into Kenyan Shillings (KSh).
✅ Created a Full Name column
=CONCAT(B2," ",C2)

After verifying the results, the original First Name and Last Name columns were hidden since the information was now represented in the Full Name column.
✅ Improved worksheet readability
Adjusted column widths to ensure all data was displayed clearly.
This phase reminded me that data analysis is not only about creating charts or writing queries. The quality of insights depends heavily on the quality of the data being analyzed. Taking time to clean and document data creates a strong foundation for the next stages of the project.
The next phase will be Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), where I will start using Excel formulas, PivotTables, and charts to uncover patterns and insights from the hospital records.
articles.title: # Cleaning My Hospital Records Dataset: Preparing Data for Analysis

articles.description:
Efficiency is the goal of automation, but in high-consequence settings, full autonomy is the wrong target. Actions that change production data, move money, reconfigure network hardware or contact customers should combine the machine's speed with verified human judgment. The principle is Human First, Machine Second.
In plain terms: A junior colleague can read, research and draft all day without asking. But before they wire money or delete a database, they get a sign-off from someone senior.
Divide actions into two classes with automatic gates.
Reversible, low-impact (fully autonomous): reading documentation, summarising logs, querying read-only metrics, drafting a remediation plan.
Irreversible or high-impact (gated): dropping a table, changing a switch VLAN, deploying to production, approv…
articles.title: Day 28: Human-in-the-Loop Architecture — Machine Second, Human First in Practice

I pressed Stop on a task. When I looked 35 seconds later, a file in my test folder was gone.
The file was keep.txt, the folder was throwaway, and I had told the agent to set the trap itself: nohup sh -c 'sleep 20; rm keep.txt' > /dev/null 2>&1 &. Stop was supposed to end everything the task had started. It ended Claude Code, and the rm ran anyway. Of the bugs my end-to-end runs found in the wrapper app, this is the one that deleted a file.
This is part 9 of a series about Refmade, a desktop app I'm building alone. Refmade lets people who don't live in a terminal hand work to the Claude Code or Codex they have already installed, and shows the agents as an office you can watch.
